Should I buy shares in M&G right now?
A tie-up with the Japanese insurance giant Dai-ichi Life is a vote of confidence that could make the UK investment manager an attractive proposition
It’s been a soggy ride for M&G investors in the six years since it was demerged from Prudential. The shares of the UK life insurance and asset management company have spent most of the period below their debut price of 220p, though the consolation has been a generous dividend.
Arguably, the company made one of its biggest strategic moves last week when it revealed a tie-up with the Japanese insurance giant Dai-ichi Life. Dai-ichi is to buy a 15 per cent stake in M&G, take a seat on the M&G board, and will put $6 billion of business M&G’s way over five years.
The verdict so far has been mildly positive. The shares are up to 239p, which is pretty much their highest since Andrea Rossi took over as chief executive in October 2022. Analysts at JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and BNP Paribas all have a buy rating on the shares.
Certainly, the operating benefits from the new deal are clear. M&G will become Dai-ichi’s preferred fund management partner in Europe. Half of the targeted $6 billion of inflows will come from Dai-ichi’s own balance sheet and half will come from the distribution of M&G products by Dai-ichi advisers.
At least $3 billion of the new business will be ploughed into M&G’s “high alpha” strategies in public and private markets — funds where the fees tend to be higher.
M&G will gain access to Dai-ichi’s distribution networks both in Japan and other parts of Asia. There are also collaboration opportunities across life insurance, including in pension risk transfer: M&G re-entered the lucrative bulk purchase annuities business in 2023 and Dai-ichi is starting to sniff out the possibility of writing annuities now that interest rates in Tokyo are heading into positive territory for the first time in years.
Dai-ichi’s choice of M&G is a vote of confidence in the London-based company. Dai-ichi is one of the biggest life assurers in Japan with more than £300 billion of assets and a market value of about £22 billion. Its own share price performance has been far stronger than M&G’s in recent years.
But the stakebuilding aspect of the alliance is more double-edged. Dai-ichi has promised to go no higher than 20 per cent. It has also agreed not to disturb the natural day-to-day share price too much by limiting daily purchases to no more than 25 per cent of the average daily volume.
Even so, that 15 per cent holding could be seen as a bit of a poison pill, making it harder for anyone else to make a bid for M&G. Schroders took a serious look in 2020 before walking away on worries about a clash of cultures between the two businesses. Macquarie, the Australian investment group, was also rumoured to have sniffed around in 2023. Dai-ichi’s stake would make any bid for M&G by a rival considerably more difficult.
M&G has struggled to shake off its image as a stodgy life company with an asset management arm that continues to suffer from client defections. Rossi has fixed some of the basic problems by strengthening the balance sheet, simplifying the operating model and trimming away at costs. But the shift to more of a growth agenda has yet to convince investors.
The Dai-ichi alliance won’t immediately boost M&G profits by more than a percentage point or two, but it should help improve the pro-growth credentials of the company and perhaps pave the way for a valuation reset. M&G is not just an investor in lower-margin bonds and equities. After some tactical acquisitions, it now has £74 billion of its £315 billion of assets under management in more fashionable private markets, where the fees are higher
The shares remain relatively cheap, trading at about 8.5 times forecast profits for 2026. That compares with about 9.5 times for the sector as a whole. The yield remains a very decent 8.5 per cent. The shares look attractive at this level.
One cautionary note on the Dai-ichi deal: the Japanese giant has been here before, securing a similar alliance with Janus Henderson, complete with 15 per cent stake. That tie-up was abandoned in 2021 after eight years. There’s no guarantee the M&G pact will be any more lasting.
Advice: Buy
Why: Juicy dividend combined with hopes for growth from private assets and the new Asia alliance

M&G banks on the benefits of greener housing
Greencore has a positive environmental story to tell but believes its bottom line is equally attractive to investors. One City stalwart is in for £65 million
Monday March 09 2026, 6.02am,
“This isn’t about fluffing along doing ESG stuff,” says Jon Di-Stefano, the amiable chief executive of Greencore, one of Britain’s greenest housebuilders.
He constructs one, two, three and four-bedroom homes that claim to lock up more carbon in the natural building materials they use than is emitted during the building process. Sealed to Passivhaus standards and loaded with heat pumpsand solar panels, they are also cheap to run, enabling Greencore homes to command a premium price when sold on the market.
The environmental, social and governance fluffing that Di-Stefano is distancing himself from is the suggestion that one of the country’s largest City investors has backed Greencore with £65 million of British savers’ money because the optics make them look good.
M&G Investments, which manages most of M&G’s £130 billion long-term savings and investment fund, owns 80 per cent of Greencore. It has taken the stake through its venture fund, called Catalyst, which has invested just over £1 billion since its launch in 2021 in private companies that promise to deliver “both financial returns and measurable social and environmental impact”.
There is no doubt that Greencore has a positive environmental story to tell. Its clever, factory-made lime-hemp and wood-fibre insulation and timber walls are an innovation that its co-founder Ian Pritchett developed over 30 years of working with traditional materials. The 300mm external walls, fitted to a floor plate on site to 1mm precision, give Greencore’s homes an aesthetic and energy efficient profile that makes them stand out from much of the rest of the market.
But Greencore also intends to deliver those M&G savers a good return. Based on its five-year business plan, it could be worth £400 million by the mid-2030s. Before then it aims to pay dividends. It will break even when it builds 200 homes a year — expected sometime in 2027 — and by the early 2030s it should be making £30 million profit a year.
In the past, modular building companies have struggled to build and sell enough homes to cover their costs
“Housebuilding, if you get it right, is a profitable business. Our business plan, which I think is reasonable rather than ridiculous, gets to over £30 million of profit in five years’ time,” says Di-Stefano, a former executive at the London high-rise builder Telford Homes. “In theory, [M&G] could take out 80 per cent of the profit, or they could reinvest it and grow the business even more, and maybe sell at some point.”
Greencore has learnt from the experiences of the first generation of modular building companies, such as TopHat, Ilke Homes and Legal & General’s modular arm. These firms invested heavily in their off-site factories but struggled to build and sell enough homes to cover their costs.
Off-site preparation at Greencore
At Greencore, the off-site preparation is limited to the exterior and internal walls, with everything put together on site rather than ferried along a motorway on wide-load lorries that require police escorts. The partial prefabrication means Greencore homes take two months less to build than their brick-based peers.
The relationship between the small builder and the City suits runs deep. Di-Stefano says M&G’s 150-strong real estate team has also bought several dozen affordable homes on Greencore’s site in Launton, near Bicester, Oxfordshire. One of its senior team, Alex Greaves, is also a non-executive director.
“They care about what we are doing. The good thing about that is sometimes things do go wrong, but they are with you on the journey,” says Di-Stefano.
Niranjan Sirdeshpande, who heads M&G’s Catalyst team, appears to care deeply. Unlike most cautious City money men, he talks like an operator, rather than an investor. M&G first invested in 2022, after Greencore had built its first small development at Springfield Meadows in Southmoor, near Oxford.
“The challenge was that they were not operating at an institutional scale and for a housebuilder to operate at institutional scale it is a long, patient game,” he says.
“Luckily”, M&G’s funds think long term. To move from a tiny operation to a more substantial one, Greencore has to shift from its “scrappy” initial operating model to a more professional one. M&G invested £1 million in its new factory, where the walls are built, and also recruited new managers, including Di-Stefano, who have experience of building homes on a large scale.
“That matters because it tells you what you need to succeed and you can put those processes and practices in place,” says Sirdeshpande.
M&G’s backing also helped win over banks, subcontractors and landowners, who might not fancy selling sites to an unproven newcomer. From holding no land for development, it is now taking enough for 2,200 homes through various stages of the planning system.
Builders aren’t building – and that’s a worry for the economy
Sometimes the vision held by management and owner diverges. Di-Stefano sees merit in focusing their expansion plans on areas in and around the Oxford to Cambridge corridor, where demand for new homes is strong and economic development is high on planning department agendas. Given their relatively small size, he is relaxed about rival green housebuilders copying their approach and setting up in other parts of the country.
“The industry is supposed to be delivering 300,000 homes a year, [but is] nowhere near that. And we [Greencore] are delivering 100. Even in our wildest dreams we are at 1,200, 1,300 a year. So if someone else starts doing [what they are doing] it isn’t actually that big a deal. I don’t think they even will, because the industry is terrible at taking on change.”
Di-Stefano is also wary of taking on too many fixed costs too quickly. “You can do too much. I think we have the balance right,” he says.
Sirdeshpande, on the other hand, sees Greencore as a future national housebuilder. “We want to take this model to multiple parts of the UK. Today they largely operate in the home counties, but one of the great things about the business is that you can set up a manufacturing facility for under £2 million. It means from an execution perspective, as you start to really win large land banks you can set up a hub and spoke model where you have localised manufacturing of these houses.”
He also sees other investors joining M&G on Greencore’s share register as the business grows. “We will continue to lead future rounds. Where possible we will bring in external investors,” he says, speculating that local authority pension funds might want to get involved on a project-by-project basis.
M&G is a signatory of the Mansion House accord, which is a voluntary commitment for 17 pension funds to invest at least 10 per cent of defined contribution funds in private markets by 2030, with at least 5 per cent of the total allocated to the UK.
The surprising part of M&G’s support for Greencore is quite how early in the company’s development it has got involved. Normally City investors look to deploy large sums of capital in more mature companies that can spend it sensibly and without suffering indigestion.
Operating at this micro-level “is new for M&G”, admits Sirdeshpande, but he says it is important for investors to “roll up their sleeves” and help promising small companies become large ones.
M&G has always been an “active” investor, he adds. “This is us expressing that earlier in the value chain. In my view it is easier to build the right foundations and then build up from there rather than go into a larger business, where you own 5 per cent, and try to get them to change things. [Here] the founders or management teams want advice. They want to know if they execute on a plan, in five to seven years how will the markets perceive me? What narrative should I build for the markets to be welcoming of my business and strategy, in either the public credit side or public equity side if I want to list this business?”
Again, Sirdeshpande is thinking big. Greencore becoming a £400 million company is a good result. But how can it breach the hallowed $1 billion mark and keep on growing, he wonders. “The difference between selling at $1 billion and having a multibillion-dollar business in the UK is really about having ambitious people running that business, ambitious investors backing that business, saying we will continue to back you in the long run.”

M&G fund dominates allocators’ emerging market debt exposure
​
Summarise
​
If a storm it indeed be, then the crisis in the gulf has emerging market assets right at the eye of it.
Investors reacted to the geopolitical uncertainty in a very traditional way by piling into the dollar as a safe haven asset, reversing a period of decline for the greenback relative to peer currencies.
And its an adage almost as old as some of my jokes that when the dollar strengthens, emerging market asset prices fall, whether the fundamentals justify it or not.
So if turbulence be afoot for the asset class we thought we would have a peek at our proprietary database to see which fund managers are most trusted by DFMs to navigate the uncertainty.
When it comes to emerging market debt, there is quite the convergence around M&G’s Emerging Market bond fund, which appears in 10 portfolios, to wrap some context around that, only 21 funds in the sector are owned by anyone.
The M&G fund was once run by Claudia Calich, a doyen of the asset class, and on her retirement last year it passed to Carlos Carranza, her long standing deputy.
Performance has been strong, it is about £1.1bn in size and has returned 27 per cent over the past five years, compared with 19 per cent for the sector.
Investors may also be reassured by the fact its top quartile over the past six months, the period with the new manager at the helm.
Next most owned is, rather surprisingly given the asset class in question, an index fund.
This is Legal and General’s Emerging Market Government Bond fund, which appears in three portfolios.
An important factor here may be that the Legal and General fund buys emerging market debt denominated in dollars, rather than local currency, and so may prove more resilient than the local currency equivalent funds if the greenback’s rise proves to be persistent.
It is just over £1bn in size and has 471 holdings, among the largest are Brazilian government bonds and those may prove resilient if oil and commodity prices remain high.
The index has not been a buoyant source of returns over the past five years, returning 10 per cent compared with 13 per cent for the peer group average.
Barings Emerging Market Debt Blended fund and Morgan Stanley’s Emerging Market debt fund are the only other mandates to appear in more than one portfolio.
The Barings fund is less than £220mn in size while the Morgan Stanley product is £250mn in size, the Luxembourg-domiciled vehicle has beaten the benchmark over the past three years.

Private markets power M&G £10bn flow turnaround
​
The asset manager returned to positive inflows in 2025, with its private credit arm playing a big role in the firm's £7.8bn haul during the year.
M&G returned to positive inflows in 2025 with its private markets franchise powering the major turnaround.
Overall M&G generated a net inflow of £7.8bn from open business in 2025, reversing the £1.9bn outflow it suffered in 2024.
Flows into asset management stood at £7bn in 2025, of which private markets accounted for £3.9bn. Private and structured credit accounted for the bulk of this inflow at £2.8bn.
Of the £3.1bn inflow generated by public markets, M&G said it had seen strong demand for high alpha strategies, alongside increased appetite for European and Asian strategies. It added that impact and sustainability remain a priority for institutional clients.
There were also green shoots in its UK business, which posted inflows of £300m compared to an outflow of £4.7bn in 2024.
Assets under management across the business rose from £345.9bn to £375.9bn, with its private assets franchise accounting for £81bn of this. Assets in its international business rose from £89bn to £107bn. International clients now make up 59% of externally managed assets, up from 56%.
Adjusted operating pre-tax profit edged up by £1m over the year to £838m.
Prufund flows turn positive
After suffering an outflow of £0.6bn in the first six months of 2025, the Prufund pulled in £406m in the second half, recording a positive net inflow every month from July to December.
M&G has extended the £68bn smoothed fund range’s reach through signing distribution agreements in Switzerland and the UAE.
The firm is also working to launch the Prufund on FNZ platforms, giving it access to the digital platform market, creating a new distribution channel for retail investors and customers.
At the end of last year M&G partnered with Dai-ichi Life, giving the asset manager access to the significant distribution network of a major Japanese life insurer. As part of the deal, Dai-ichi agreed to take a 15% stake in M&G. By the end of the year, the Japanese firm owned 9.6% of M&G shares.
M&G CEO Andrea Rossi described 2025 as one of ‘strong commercial momentum and strategic progress’.
‘We continued to invest in our business, setting it up for long-term growth and expanding our international distribution and investment capabilities,’ Rossi said.
‘We delivered £7.8bn of net inflows from open business, an improvement of nearly £10 billion year-on-year, driven by a strong performance in asset management and a return to growth in life.
‘With a clear strategy and the right resources in place, I am confident in M&G’s ability to deliver meaningful profit acceleration and sustainable long-term value for customers, clients and shareholders.’
Shortly after 9am shares in M&G had dipped by 1.2% to 297p.

M&G's PruFund returns to inflow of £200m
​
PruFund, a flagship product for M&G, returned to a net inflow position in the second half of 2025 following improved market conditions.
M&G’s PruFund range has returned to net inflows of £200m up from outflows of £900m in 2024, despite it not being launched on FNZ platforms yet.
In its full year results for 2025, PruFund, a flagship product for M&G, returned to a net inflow position in the second half of 2025 following improved market conditions.
Despite CEO Andrea Rossi telling Citywire in September that the range would be launched on FNZ platforms early this year, it is understood this has yet to happen.
Its results said ‘integration of PruFund on FNZ technology will enable access to the digital platform market’. One source familiar with the business told Citywire that it is still being built.
M&G’s overall life business, which includes its wealth, annuities and the PruFund range, saw £800m of net inflows up from £1bn outflows the year previous.
M&G said the position reflected the bulk purchase annuities transactions which contributed £1.5bn inflows and an improvement in PruFund outflows during the year.
‘The reduction in net outflows reflects a return to a net inflow position in the second half of the year following a recovery in the markets after volatility earlier in the year,’ M&G said.
The M&G Wealth platform business has had a turbulent couple of years, with a failed sale and threats of a wind down which saw advisers leave the platform. In its overall platform and advice business there were outflows of £28m in 2025, down slightly from the year previous which saw outflows of £31m.
It said: ‘Increased outflows from our adviser platform business, following our strategic repositioning announced in 2024 and expected run-off from our other small closed books of business offset the net client inflows from open business.’
In October last year, Citywire reported that M&G is in advanced talks with SS&C Hubwise to outsource its platform operations after a sale process that dragged on for nearly two years failed to find a buyer.

M&G flows turn positive as firm grows international clients
​
Summarise
​
Tara O'Connor
M&G saw flows swing back to positive in 2025 following growth with its international client base, its annual results show.
Article continues after advert
The results, published today (March 12), showed the company recorded £7.8bn net flows in the year, compared with £1.9bn of outflows in 2024.
M&G said this change was driven by its asset management arm and a return to growth in its life business.
Total assets under management stood at £375.9bn for the year, up from £345.9bn.
There were £7bn of net inflows in asset management, representing 4.4 per cent of total AUM.
And, almost 60 per cent of its asset management AUM comes from international clients, a rise of 37 per cent compared with five years ago.
Andrea Rossi, group CEO, said: “In Life, we materially increased bulk purchase annuity (BPA) volumes, and brought PruFund back into sustained net inflows in the second half.
“We expect this momentum across the business to continue in 2026, as we move forward on our growth journey also leveraging our recently launched With-Profits BPA proposition.
“With a clear strategy and the right resources in place, I am confident in M&G’s ability to deliver meaningful profit acceleration and sustainable long-term value for customers, clients and shareholders.”
It also announced a total dividend of 20.5p per share, up 2 per cent on last year’s 20.1p.
In 2025, M&G managed to make £250mn of cost savings, which it said beat its target.
In January, the company appointed a new chief transformation officer, Simon Tasker.

M&G returns to positive flows as it targets overseas clients
M&G has returned to positive flows after expanding its offering to international clients.
In its full financial results, published today (12 March), the FTSE 100 savings and investment group said assets under management and administration (AUMA) continued to grow through 2025, reaching around £364.9bn by the end of September.
The company, which serves around 4.5 million retail clients globally, is positioning itself as a diversified investment platform spanning public markets, private assets and insurance solutions.
A key theme in the report is the return to positive flows from M&G’s “open business”, which includes asset management and wealth products distributed to external clients.
In the first half of 2025, the firm recorded £2.1bn of net inflows, reversing the outflows seen in the same period the previous year.
Within this, the asset management division delivered £2.6bn of inflows from external investors, reflecting stronger demand for its strategies and improving investment performance.
By the end of the third quarter, total net inflows from open business had reached £3.9bn for the year.
Another key trend is the increasing importance of overseas clients.
International investors now account for around 58% of asset management AUMA, compared with just 37% five years ago.
This diversification has helped M&G reduce reliance on the UK retail market and expand distribution of its funds globally.
The report also emphasises M&G’s push into private assets such as private credit, infrastructure and real estate.
Private markets now account for roughly a quarter of the group’s assets, reflecting a strategic shift towards fewer liquid investments that can offer diversification and potentially higher yields.
Demand for these strategies has been strong, with private markets AUM growing by more than £5bn over the past year as investors search for alternatives to traditional public market exposures.
M&G has also strengthened its international relationships, most notably through a strategic partnership with Japanese insurer Dai-ichi Life.
The agreement includes a 15% equity investment in M&G and commitments for at least $6bn of allocations into M&G funds over five years, alongside a further $2bn of potential new business flows.
Such partnerships are intended to provide more stable institutional capital while expanding distribution in Asia and other global markets.
Alongside growth initiatives, the firm has continued its multi-year cost-reduction programme.
M&G has already delivered over £200m of cost savings as part of a wider restructuring aimed at simplifying the business and improving margins.
Chief executive Andrea Rossi has said the firm is entering a “new phase” focused on sustainable growth across both asset management and life operations.

Panasonic scheme secures £140m buy-in with M&G
‘Streamlined’ transaction secures the benefits of around 650 scheme members
The Panasonic UK Pension Plan has completed a £140m buy-in deal with M&G.

Inside M&G’s £130bn with-profits fund as clients share £3.2bn bonus
​
Summarise
​
David Thorpe
The two million clients in M&G’s with-profits fund, which includes PruFund, will split a bonus pool of £3.2bn for the year, after the fund gained 9.6 per cent after tax in 2025.
Article continues after advert
Three different types of client are eligible for a share of the bonus pot.
There are those who made a one-off investment in a with-profits bond, those who invested via a personal pension in the with-profits fund, and those who bought an annuity via the Prudential Guaranteed Income Plan.
The latter group have not previously received a bonus, but this year will receive 0.45 per cent of their investment as a lump sum. That product only launched in 2025.
In investment terms, the fund has produced an annualised return over the past decade of 9.17 per cent, compared with 4.94 per cent for the peer group.
M&G states the annual bonus usually means clients see the value of their plan rise by between 6 and 9 per cent, separate from any regular income they receive.
Clive Bolton, chief executive of M&G Life, said: “Through the strength and scale of the with-profits fund, I’m delighted we can share around £3.2bn in bonuses with about two million of our customers this year.
“In a period marked by geopolitical and economic uncertainty, customers are seeking confidence in their investment managers to deliver reliable, stable and smooth investment returns over the long-term.
“Our purpose is to give people real confidence to put their money to work and this bonus declaration is testament to that commitment.”
The investment department is run by Ciaran Mulligan, chief investment officer at M&G Life.
About 80 per cent of the assets within the fund are run by other fund managers within M&G.
The remaining 20 per cent is running by managers from outside of M&G who are selected and monitored by Mulligan’s team. These tend to be in asset classes such as US Smaller Companies or if the internal M&G managers have capacity issues.
Mulligan has a group of 10 people in a “manager oversight team” to monitor the fund managers both within other departments of M&G and elsewhere.
He said the key to delivering investment performance in a multi-asset fund is to have as many sources of return as possible.
The investments
The with-profits fund has investments ranging from the Arndale shopping centre in Manchester, to an early stage biotech business in Cambridge, and a music royalties business called Seeker, in which M&G’s with-profits fund has $300mn (£222mn) invested. It generates £17mn of annual revenue for the portfolio.
Seeker is run by a Grammy award winning songwriter, whose work has been performed by Beyoncé, as well as other stars.
Among the song rights owned by Seeker Music is “A Bar Song” by Shaboozey.
The PruFund Growth fund has UK equities as its largest exposure, at 12 per cent of the total, while 8 per cent is in UK Real Estate, and 7.2 per cent in US equities.
The breadth of the holdings can be seen in the fact that 1.2 per cent of the fund’s capital is in African bonds, a greater proportion than is in US or European high yield.
The PruFund Cautious fund has just under 10 per cent in Asian bonds as the largest holding, with UK and US investment grade bonds just behind.
Mulligan said unquoted and unlisted investments such as those mentioned above, are brought to him by other managers within M&G who are specialists in that area of investing.
He said the rise in the number of private markets funds meant there was likely to be a “wider dispersion” in the returns achieved by such funds, with some performing very well, and others very poorly.
He said: “Although there is a lot of interest in private investments right now, we are fortunate that this is an area that the wider M&G Group has been investing in for decades.
“It is important to have multiple sources of returns, and being able to invest in assets that a private individual cannot access, and as a source of returns they cannot otherwise access.”

Expecto return-um’: M&G cashes in on new Harry Potter store
​
Summarise
​
The new Oxford Street store will follow similar projects in New York, Chicago and Tokyo.
A central London property redevelopment, backed by M&G’s £130bn With Profits fund, is being used as the UK’s first Harry Potter flagship store.
The two floor property, based at the £250m redevelopment named The Ribbon on Oxford Street, will be leased to Warner Brothers. The shop opening follows similar openings in New York, Chicago and Tokyo.
Ciaran Mulligan, CIO at M&G Life, said: ‘This deal shows how the high street can bring some magic to your pension investments.
‘Through the scale of the With Profits fund, we can take on major redevelopments like this and turn historic sites into vibrant destinations that support our customers for years to come. By working closely with the real estate asset management team, we’re helping to bring new life to Oxford Street’
The real estate investment is part of M&G With Profits’ large allocation to private markets, which amounts to around £30bn of its allocation. In January the With Profits vehicle seeded a new infrastructure fund that backs social projects.

M&G to enter €2bn CLO ETF market with new active product
​
Summarise
​
Revealed: Investment manager will launch a new ETF targeting low-risk credit exposure to Europe's securitisation market.
M&G is set launch a new active exchange-traded fund (ETF) vying for exposure to European collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), Citywire understands.
The new product, which is expected to be named ‘M&G European AAA CLO Active Ucits ETF’, will likely target exposure to AAA-grade CLO tranches.
CLOs are made up of investment-grade corporate loans that have been bundled together and split into different tranches based on their risk level, with AAA having the lowest risk of default payment.
Ucits rules limit CLO ETFs to AAA/AA exposure only, and not to lower-rate tranches, which can offer higher yields but carry higher default risks.
The European CLO ETF market currently sits at around €2bn assets under management (AUM), up from €382.9m just one year ago, according to Morningstar data.
Asset managers have been looking to take a slice of the market with new launches. State Street and BlackStone entered in September, and private credit boutique Muzinich to launch a CLO ETF filed to launch a strategy in February.
The recent uptick in CLO ETF launches also followed a call from the European Commission (EC) to ‘strengthen the EU securitisation market’.
This ETF will be M&G’s fifth ETF product in the European market, after launching its maiden range in December with three fixed income products and one equity.

M&G completes illiquid asset transfer to secure £60m BPA deal
​
Summarise
​
Transaction with unnamed scheme secures the benefits of over 750 members
The transaction was completed by M&G's wholly-owned subsidiary Prudential Assurance Company and was made possible through the insurer's with-profits fund entering into a market transaction at the same time to purchase an illiquid asset in-specie from the pension scheme.
M&G said its ability to invest in illiquid assets through its with-profits fund "enabled a mutually beneficial solution to be created for the fund, the scheme and its members".
The trustee was advised during the process by Gallagher, with the firm acting as risk transfer broker after its appointment in 2025. Independent Governance Group (IGG) was independent trustee to the pension scheme and Sackers provided legal advice.
Trustee chair (of IGG) Roger Mattingly said: "We are pleased to have partnered with M&G on this transaction. Its bespoke solution in addressing the trustee's illiquid asset challenge was instrumental in achieving the objectives of both the trustee and the sponsor.
"I would like to extend my gratitude to our risk transfer adviser, Gallagher, whose expert guidance, and strong project management ensured a seamless and efficient process. I would also like to thank our legal adviser, Sackers, for its clear and pragmatic advice throughout. This collaboration has delivered a fantastic outcome for the long-term security of member benefits."
M&G head of bulk annuity origination and execution Rosie Fantom added: "We are delighted to partner with the trustee to help secure the long-term financial future of more than 750 members.
"This transaction exemplifies how we can deliver tailored solutions for schemes of all sizes facing particular challenges, by drawing on the strength and flexibility of our wider business. By accepting the illiquid asset in-specie, in a mutually beneficial transaction, we were able to resolve a major obstacle for the trustee, allowing the pension scheme and sponsor to reduce risks by insuring members' benefits. We look forward to supporting more schemes as they navigate their de-risking journeys and achieve greater certainty for members."
Gallagher senior risk transfer actuary Callum Slattery commented: "It was a privilege to advise the trustee on this unique transaction. M&G demonstrated a willingness to understand the scheme's specific needs and work creatively with the trustee to address the challenge posed by the scheme's illiquid assets. A surge in the price of Brent crude from just over $72 a barrel to almost $120 sparked a rout in government bonds in the early weeks of the Iran conflict, as traders bet a sharp pick-up in inflation would prevent central bankers from cutting interest rates and could force some to raise them.
That pushed yields on 10-year Treasuries up more than 0.5 percentage points to a high of nearly 4.5 per cent, while the equivalent yields on gilts jumped nearly 0.9 percentage points to more than 5.1 per cent.
However, yields have since come off their conflict highs — despite another burst of volatility on Thursday following US President Donald Trump’s threats to escalate attacks on Iran — as some managers point to the start of a shift in investors’ focus towards growth concerns.
“The growth risks are real,” said Andrew Sheets, global head of fixed income research at Morgan Stanley, which moved to a bullish recommendation on US Treasuries at the end of last week “on the belief that the market previously had been overly focused on inflation risks” and was not reflecting the hit to demand.
Iain Stealey, international chief investment officer for global fixed income at JPMorgan Asset Management, said he had been buying long-term debt in Europe, Asia and North America.
The “knee-jerk reaction” to focus on inflation was “probably overdone”, he said. “If you are a central banker today, the most obvious thing you would do is wait and see.”
Schroders had bought Canadian government bonds in recent weeks, in a bet that interest rate rises priced in by the market were “inconsistent with the economic fundamentals”, according to strategist James Bilson, who pointed to a soft labour market and a cooling economy.
Some managers argue that bonds will perform well, whether or not the war ends quickly.
Bonds present value whether there was “de-escalation from here or, on the other hand, a significant escalation or policy error-induced growth scare”, said Arun Sai, senior multi-asset strategist at Pictet Asset Management.
Jamie Searle, European rates strategist at Citi, said that even if there was a quick de-escalation of the conflict, “there would still be significant uncertainty over long-term disruption to energy supply [and] the market should pivot more to pricing the medium-term growth consequences”.
Surging oil and gas prices have driven up short-term inflation expectations across the globe, with one-year US inflation swaps going from about 2.5 per cent at the outbreak of the conflict to just above 3.1 per cent.
But longer-term market expectations for US inflation have not kept up. The so-called five-year, five-year — which shows expectations for inflation over a five-year period starting in half a decade’s time — is little changed at about 2.4 per cent.

M&G’s role in Shaboozey’s success is down to a business called Seeker Music, which the fund manager set up in 2020 with a view to investing in the music industry.

Seeker also has a strategy of finding ways to “flip”, or interpolate, songs into formats modern audiences would prefer.

He remembers loving J-Kwon’s tune 20 years ago. “When that song came on in the clubs, people just lost their minds, at least in Los Angeles,” said Bogart, 47.

M&G could have achieved exposure to the music industry by investing in funds such as Hipgnosis Songs Fund, founded by Merck Mercuriadis and Nile Rodgers, which used to be listed in London but has since been taken private by the private equity firm Blackstone; or Round Hill Music, which was also listed in London until two years ago; or other private equity firms such as Lyric Capital Group.

It previously said it was targeting a mid-teen internal rate of return — a measure of profitability — from its investment by the time it makes its exit.

How to beat the pension tax raid on salary sacrifice

Summarise

Budget changes that will mean many pension savers paying more national insurance do not kick in until 2029, so there’s still time to boost your pot.
The amount workers can pay into a pension free of national insurance is to be limited under the chancellor’s cap on salary sacrifice schemes.
In her second budget Rachel Reeves said that from April 2029 workers will only be able to pay up to £2,000 a year into their pension via salary sacrifice without paying national insurance on that contribution. Any pension payments above that amount will incur national insurance contributions of 8 per cent on income between £12,571 and £50,270 a year and 2 per cent on income above that.
It means that millions of workers could see their take-home pay fall as their national insurance payments increase. But with the changes not happening for more than three years, there’s still time to make the most of salary sacrifice while you can.

Lisa Picardo from the pensions consolidation firm PensionBee said: “Workers have a valuable window. Anyone who can afford to may want to increase or max out their salary sacrifice contributions this tax year, then scale back once the cap comes in.”
Here’s what you need to know.
How much extra to put in
Most pension savers can put a maximum of £60,000 (or up to 100 per cent of their earnings, whichever is lower) into their pot each tax year and get tax relief on those contributions. All pension contributions get income tax relief, either at source or claimed back through a self assessment tax return, but pension payments made through salary sacrifice also completely avoid national insurance — at the moment. Salary sacrifice involves giving up part of your gross salary, before tax or national insurance payments are taken, to go into your pension.
If you get a bonus on top of your salary, then paying that into your pension via salary sacrifice is an “easy win” according to Picardo, especially if the bonus would otherwise tip you into a higher tax bracket.
“It would mean you keep far more of the money while giving your future self a meaningful boost,” Picardo said. “Even a one-off bonus redirected now can grow substantially over the long term.”
She advised anyone paying into a pension pot to check whether their employer uses salary sacrifice.
“If it is available, acting before April 2029 will ensure that you take full advantage of the existing tax and national insurance savings for the next few tax years,” she said.
Nicholas Nesbitt from the wealth manager Forvis Mazars said: “Come 2029, this will disproportionately hit those earning less than £50,270 a year because they will be paying 8 per cent national insurance on money that they are trying to save for their future. Higher earners will be paying 2 per cent national insurance.”
Businesses also make savings from salary sacrifice because they don’t have to pay employers national insurance on the salary that employees sacrifice.
“Many companies pass on the employer national insurance contributions they save through salary sacrifice as further contributions for their employees, so removing this saving could harm workers’ pensions further.
“But a lot can change in three and a half years. While workers should plan for the changes, the landscape may be different by April 2029.”
Les Cameron from the wealth manager M&G said many workers won’t be able to afford to make greater use of salary sacrifice before the changes. “Many employees may not have the financial flexibility to increase contributions significantly, but those who can may wish to, especially if they are planning to retire in the short term.”
How much you could lose
The Times calculator shows that someone earning £50,000 a year who was contributing 5 per cent of their salary to a pension through salary sacrifice would lose out on £1,964 over ten years because of the cap.
Increasing the amount they pay into their pot over the 28 months until April 2029 by £70 a month (including tax relief) would offset the loss.
A worker earning £75,000 would lose £4,807 over ten years. They would need to pay £172 a month extra including tax relief to offset the loss.
Jon Greer from the wealth manager Quilter said: “We’re already sleepwalking into a retirement crisis. What the smorgasbord approach fails to recognise is that small tweaks can have huge behavioural impacts — and this one could harm millions of future retirements.”

M&G warns of capital hit from ground rent cap
​
The Government’s proposed cap on ground rents has triggered warnings over growing political risk in UK investment assets, after M&G revealed the reforms would deliver a £230m hit to its Group Solvency II own funds and dent long-term capital generation.
Under proposals announced today (27 January), existing annual ground rents in England and Wales would be capped at £250 from 2028, before being reduced to zero after a 40-year transition period.
M&G said it has direct exposure of £722m to ground rent assets through the shareholder fund of Prudential Assurance Company, with the reforms expected to reduce its shareholder Solvency II coverage ratio by around one percentage point.
If implemented in their current form, the changes would trigger a £230m one-off reduction in Solvency II own funds, with the impact on the Group’s solvency surplus limited to £140m, after allowing for the release of capital already held against regulatory risk.
From 2028, M&G expects the reforms to cut annual adjusted operating profit and underlying capital generation by around £15m, due to lower surplus assets in its annuity book, before any mitigating actions.
Despite the impact, the insurer said it remains well positioned to absorb the changes and reconfirmed its adjusted operating profit growth and capital generation targets, alongside its progressive dividend policy.
Group chief executive Andrea Rossi said while M&G supports the Government’s objective of strengthening leaseholder protections, the proposed approach risks damaging the UK’s reputation as a stable investment destination.
“We fully support the Government’s objective to strengthen leaseholder protection and tackle remaining egregious ground rents. However, we are disappointed that we have not been able to agree a proportionate solution that works for all parties,” Rossi said.
“These changes, if implemented, would negatively impact savers and companies that have chosen to invest in UK assets and set a worrying precedent for the UK’s reputation as a stable investment location.”
He added that M&G’s strong financial position and disciplined capital management meant it remained well placed to manage the impact.
The announcement highlights growing concerns across the investment industry that regulatory and political intervention is becoming a material risk factor for long-term asset allocation — particularly for insurers, pension schemes and annuity providers reliant on predictable cashflows.
Ground rents have historically been viewed as low-risk, long-duration income assets, widely held by pension funds, insurers, charities and institutional investors, due to their stable and contractual nature.
M&G warned the proposed reforms risk undermining investor confidence by retrospectively altering long-established contracts and property rights, a move critics argue could discourage long-term capital investment in UK real assets.
The Residential Freehold Association (RFA) said the proposals represent a “wholly unjustified interference with existing property rights”, warning of damaging consequences for institutional capital flows.
A spokesperson said: “If enacted, this would seriously damage investor confidence in the UK housing market and send a dangerous and unprecedented signal to the wider institutional investment sector.
“Property rights and contract law are fundamental drivers of domestic and global investor confidence in the UK. Tearing up long-established contracts risks undermining the UK’s investment reputation.”
The RFA added that the reforms could hinder the delivery of building safety remediation projects, as professional freeholders are forced to exit the sector.
However, leasehold reform specialists Homehold said while the £250 cap represents progress for leaseholders, the slow pace of reform continues to frustrate homeowners.
Managing director Linz Darlington said: “A cap at £250 is a sensible choice. It recognises that freeholders will continue to receive an income stream in the short term, while ensuring leaseholders are protected from excessive charges.
“But the speed of leasehold reform remains glacial. Much of the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 is still not implemented, 18 months after Royal Assent.”
Darlington warned that without rapid legislative progress, leaseholders would see little immediate benefit, despite the scale of the political commitments.

M&G leads $50m funding round for Cambridge bio spinout
Bit.bio, whose lab-grown human brain cells have been used to create a ‘biological computer’, has secured funds from investors to expand
A University of Cambridge spinout whose lab-grown human brain cells have been used to create a “biological computer” has raised $50 million from investors to expand globally.
Bit.bio, a synthetic biology company, has also hired Lord Prior of Brampton, a former health minister and former chairman of NHS England, as its chairman as part of the fundraising round.
M&G, the asset manager and life insurer, is leading the round with a $32 million investment in the expectation that the biotech will eventually join a stock market. Blackrock is also providing a $20 million venture debt facility.
Przemek Obloj, chief executive of Bit.bio, said the cash would enable it to hire an international sales team, to further develop its data science capabilities and to launch new products.
“What Europe really needs is scale-up capital because we have a ton of great science, some really good entrepreneurs and we have some amazing teams working on it all. We get a lot of stuff to a couple of hundred million [revenues] in scale and then it gets bought out.
“If we want to build $10 billion businesses then we need to have people who are willing to write a bigger cheque. It is very easy to raise one, two, ten million. It is incredibly difficult to raise fifties and hundreds. We got lucky in the sense that we have this support [from M&G]. I wish more people were doing it. We have the largest pension system in Europe, which right now does very little for the innovation economy.”
Bit.bio was founded by Mark Kotter, a clinical neuroscience professor at the University of Cambridge, and since becoming an independent company in 2016 it has raised more than $200 million from investors including the American fund Arch Venture Partners, BlueYard Capital of Germany and Tencent, a Chinese multinational technology conglomerate. M&G was the company’s first UK institutional investor when it took part in a $30 million round in December 2024, a year when Bit.bio generated £6.9 million in revenues.

M&G to start securities lending across its fund range
​
M&G Investments has told clients it will begin securities lending on some of its funds, which it said will add “incremental” returns for clients.
Article continues after advert
In a note sent to clients, and seen by FT Adviser, M&G said, after receiving FCA approval, from April 2 the firm will introduce a securities lending programme across its range of OEIC funds.
The letter was signed by Laurence Mumford, managing director of M&G Securities Limited.
“Funds have been selected based on a range of criteria including compatibility with the programme, assets held relative to market demand and size of the fund.”
Securities lending involves M&G’s funds receiving a fee from an investor that wants exposure to the performance of a stock or a bond without owning it.
One example of this would be a firm that wants to short sell a share.
They borrow the stock from M&G today for a fee, and promise to return it at a fixed date in future.
The investor then sells the stock, and buys it back in that set timeframe, hoping that when they buy it back it will be at a lower price than they sold it, generating a profit — minus the fee paid to M&G’s fund.
Article continues after advert
The other way it may be used is if an investor wants to gain the benefit from the future rise in the price of a stock or bond, they can pay a fee to M&G now, and get the gain on the investment in future, without ever owning it.
Selling such exposure is something income funds frequently do, as it enables them to pay a high dividend to investors.
The note shared with clients said: “M&G Investments are very experienced at securities lending with a dedicated team of three investment professionals with over 20 years of experience managing a long-standing programme for our life companies’ assets.
“We view this as an opportunity to improve client outcomes by generating incremental returns at a relatively low risk.
“It is important to note that the introduction of securities lending will not result in any changes to the fund’s investment objective, investment policies, or investment strategy and approach.”
A representative of M&G told FT Adviser that a lot of stress testing has happened and clients are covered if the entity borrowing does not return the stock being lent out.
The entities borrowing the stock from M&G are required to provide collateral.
The authorised corporate director on each of the funds will have oversight on behalf of the clients in the fund.
The M&G representative added: ““As active managers, securities lending offers appropriate client funds an opportunity to generate additional income while maintaining the same investment approach and risk profile.”

Investment manager M&G returned to positive flows in 2025 as pre-tax profits remained almost unchanged.
In its 2025 results today (12 March), M&G reported net flows of £7.8bn in 2025, a turnaround from the £1.9bn of outflows in 2024.
Pre-tax profit edged up by just £1m from £837m in 2024 to £838m last year, while dividend per share also grew incrementally from 20.1p to 20.5p.
The firm's assets under management rose as well, from £345.9bn to £375.9bn last year.
Operating capital generation, however, fell year-on-year, from £933m in 2024 to £765m last year and total capital generation also dropped from over £1.1bn to £833m.
M&G highlighted how it managed to deliver "resilient performance despite volatile environment" and achieved £250m of cost savings from its transformation programme.
In the asset management division of the business, the company pulled in £7bn of net inflows from external clients and experiences "strong demand" for its high-value public equities and private markets strategies.
The asset management arm's international presence also expanded over the year, with non-UK third party assets jumping from £89bn at the end of 2024 to £107bn in 2025.
Headwinds in the UK also subsided somewhat, resulting in £300m of domestic net inflows, a significant improvement from the £4.7bn of net inflows reported in 2024.
Andrea Rossi, group CEO at M&G, said: "2025 was a year of strong commercial momentum and strategic progress for M&G. We continued to invest in our business, setting it up for long-term growth and expanding our international distribution and investment capabilities. In May, we also entered into a long-term strategic partnership with Dai-ichi Life HD, now our largest shareholder."
Looking to the future, Rossi said: "We expect this momentum across the business to continue in 2026, as we move forward on our growth journey also leveraging our recently launched With-Profits BPA proposition.
"With a clear strategy and the right resources in place, I am confident in M&G's ability to deliver meaningful profit acceleration and sustainable long-term value for customers, clients and shareholders."
Despite the return to positive flows, M&G shares were trading 2% down at the time of reporting, according to data from MarketWatch.

flagged_sentences.sentence: A tie-up with the Japanese insurance giant Dai-ichi Life is a vote of confidence that could make the UK investment manager an attractive proposition
It’s been a soggy ride for M&G investors in the six years since it was demerged from Prudential.
The shares of the UK life insurance and asset management company have spent most of the period below their debut price of 220p, though the consolation has been a generous dividend.
Arguably, the company made one of its biggest strategic moves last week when it revealed a tie-up with the Japanese insurance giant Dai-ichi Life.
Dai-ichi is to buy a 15 per cent stake in M&G, take a seat on the M&G board, and will put $6 billion of business M&G’s way over five years.
The verdict so far has been mildly positive.
The shares are up to 239p, which is pretty much their highest since Andrea Rossi took over as chief executive in October 2022.
M&G will become Dai-ichi’s preferred fund management partner in Europe.
Half of the targeted $6 billion of inflows will come from Dai-ichi’s own balance sheet and half will come from the distribution of M&G products by Dai-ichi advisers.

There are also collaboration opportunities across life insurance, including in pension risk transfer: M&G re-entered the lucrative bulk purchase annuities business in 2023 and Dai-ichi is starting to sniff out the possibility of writing annuities now that interest rates in Tokyo are heading into positive territory for the first time in years.
Dai-ichi has promised to go no higher than 20 per cent.
Even so, that 15 per cent holding could be seen as a bit of a poison pill, making it harder for anyone else to make a bid for M&G.
Macquarie, the Australian investment group, was also rumoured to have sniffed around in 2023.
M&G has struggled to shake off its image as a stodgy life company with an asset management arm that continues to suffer from client defections.
